question: What does SPE 162910 claim about time-rate models for unconventional wells, which of its methods held on the warehouse's wells, and what remains unresolved?

claims.text: The paper treats the Arps hyperbolic and exponential relations as the industry's standard EUR method for more than 80 years.

quotes.text: The Arps relations (hyperbolic and exponential relations) have been the standard for evaluating estimated ultimate recovery (EUR) in petroleum engineering applications for more than 80 years.

claims.text: An exponential least-squares fit over the first 48 months of a NM well gives a monthly decline of 0.03.
The paper describes the newer time-rate relations as empirical, without a direct link to reservoir engineering theory.

quotes.text: each/all of these models can only be described as empirical, there is no direct link with reservoir engineering theory, other than via analogy

claims.text: The modified hyperbolic model is a hyperbolic branch followed by an exponential branch with a constant terminal decline.

quotes.text: This relation has two (2) trends — an "initial" trend that is hyperbolic (i.e., for t<texp), and a "final" trend that is exponential (i.e., for t> texp)

claims.settlement_criterion: fit both branches on one warehouse well and confirm the switch improves the fit

claims.text: The power-law exponential model will describe the first year of NM wells better than the exponential branch does.
claims.settlement_criterion: compare PLE and exponential residuals over months 1-12 on the same wells

claims.text: Monthly rates without pressures limit the warehouse to the paper's rate-time relations; the pseudo-pressure diagnostics cannot be reproduced here.
claims.settlement_criterion: a pressure column in a future snapshot would let the diagnostic functions be computed

unresolved: Whether TX lease-level rows and well-level rows give different fitted declines for the same lease.
Which diagnostic functions can be computed from monthly rates alone.
